HEADLINE: ALP open to boosting more workers' wages
TEXT:
Labor is open to subsidising wage rises in other low-paid, female-dominated professions after promising to boost childcare workers' pay packets, emboldening unions to push for increases for aged care employees.

As both leaders campaigned in Perth, Mr Shorten said Labor picked childcare workers to receive assistance first because they were in an important sector, sparking accusations from Prime Minister Scott Morrison that Mr Shorten would set wages for other industries too if he didn't like what people were paid.

Mr Shorten unveiled plans to boost the pay of 100,000 childcare workers by $11,300 on top of award increases over the next eight years, equivalent to a 20 per cent wage rise. The subsidy pledge will cost taxpayers $537 million over the forward estimates, ballooning to $9.9 billion over the decade.

Labor argues the move will address the gender pay gap, given 96 per cent of employees in the historically low-paid childcare industry are women, while avoiding slugging parents with higher fees. But the promise has put pressure on Labor to also lift wages in other low-paying industries heavily subsidised by taxpayers, such as aged care, which employs about 360,000 people and pays between $40,000 and $48,000 a year for a full-time employee.

NSW Nurses and Midwives Association secretary Brett Holmes said "there could be similar arguments" made that aged care workers were deserving of higher pay like childcare workers. "We've been campaigning on getting enough staff and to get enough staff in aged care you need to improve pay," he said.

Other unions in the early childhood sector will press Labor for even more money. Independent Education Union federal secretary Chris Watt said Labor's $11,300 in increases "don't go anywhere near the pay equity gap for [university-educated] teachers" and his union would continue its equal pay claim for that cohort before the Fair Work Commission.

The IEU wants pay lifted from $70,000 to $100,000 for university-educated teachers in community-based, for-profit long-day care centres and those attached to non-government schools. The case covers 15,000 non-government teachers, with about 5000 in preschools who are more likely to be paid closer to $100,000. If Fair Work grants the increase, a Labor government may have to increase its funding, although the union's "conservative estimates" also calculate the wage rise could be funded by a $4 a day increase in childcare prices.

Labor's move to address childcare pay are part of a suite of measures to tackle low wages growth broadly. Retailers are bracing for wage rises of up to 21 per cent through the restoration of penalty rates, while Labor has flagged reviving the road safety remuneration tribunal, which could put up truck drivers' wages.

Pressed on why childcare workers had been singled out, Mr Shorten said they had been picked "to go first" because it was a "strategically important industry". "What could be more in the national interest than the quality care and education of our zero to five-year-olds?" he said.

"I don't see this as being economy-wide this approach, at all. But I do accept that in certain sectors of the economy we have a wages problem."

Mr Morrison said Mr Shorten was yet to explain how the extra money would be directed to childcare workers. "The other real question is this; what about construction workers, who are getting paid the same, men and women? What about people working in the retail industry? What about people who are hairdressers? Is he going to subsidise their wages," Mr Morrison said.

Key pointsLabor has unveiled plans to boost the pay of 100,000 childcare workers by $11,300.

Pressure is growing on the party to lift wages in other low-paying industries.

HEADLINE: Childcare stocks rise on Labor plan
TEXT:
The two biggest ASX-listed childcare stocks experienced a solid bounce in their share prices on Monday because of the "tailwind" from a generous taxpayer-funded childcare package announced by Labor leader Bill Shorten.

Shares in G8 Education, which runs 500 childcare centres around Australia, closed 3.4 per cent higher at $3.07 on Monday, after earlier climbing almost 6 per cent to an intra-day high of $3.14.

The shares were wallowing at $1.91 just six months ago, but the end of a childcare places oversupply had delivered extra optimism over the past few months, with the new Labor policies now adding extra zip.

Think Childcare, a mid-sized group which has just expanded into Western Australia from its traditional heartland of the eastern states, increased by 3.9 per cent to $1.75 on Monday.

The larger ASX-listed dentistry stocks also gained ground after Labor promised to spend $2.4 billion to give older people on the aged pension or Commonwealth seniors card holders up to $1000 of free dental care every two years. Pacific Smiles gained 6 per cent to $1.25, while 1300 Smiles was up slightly.

Analysts overwhelmingly believe the Labor childcare policies will be a plus for shareholders in ASX childcare groups.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Garry Sherriff said the Labor policies were likely to increase demand for childcare through more generous childcare subsidies for parents on lower income brackets. Mr Sherriff said it was "another tailwind for the sector". The proposed 20 per cent wage increase for childcare workers over and above the annual award rate rise over the next eight years, amounted to $11,300 above the award.

That cost of higher wages would be funded by the government and not the childcare operator.

Mr Sherriff said the announcements were a "net positive for listed operators" and demand for childcare places should increase if Labor wins government.

Labor has warned it would ask the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission to investigate any excessive fee increases imposed by childcare operators.

Mr Sherriff said it was likely centre operators would "act rationally" and be unlikely to lift annual prices above 3 to 4 per cent to minimise the risk of intervention by governments.

He expects G8 Education shares to rise to $3.50 over the next 12 months. RBC has a 12-month price target of $2.25 on Think Childcare.

In Sydney, Top Ryde Early Learning owner and provider Nesha Hutchinson said Mr Shorten's announcement that childcare workers should be paid more to reflect the importance of their work was "noble". Mum and dad providers who own just one or two centres make up about 85 per cent of authorised providers.

Ms Hutchinson said a price cap on the cost of childcare would not work because the costs of providing care for operators differed vastly "between Sydney and Bendigo" because of factors such as rents, and it was difficult to compare geographic locations.

Furthermore, parents might want to access additional services such as immersive French classes, but such add-ons changed the cost of care.

She said price gouging is unlikely because most childcare operators are embedded within communities and have direct relationships with families, meaning gouging wouldn't be "good mercenary practice" for long-term business success.

Ms Hutchinson, the Australian Childcare Alliance vice-president, said Labor's proposal to change the childcare subsidy thresholds would be positive in terms of making childcare more affordable for more families.

She said a pressing childcare issue that neither major party had addressed was the "activities" test, which requires parents to be working, studying or volunteering to access childcare subsidies. The "activities" test isn't always in the best interests of children, she said.

The Labor policy promises free childcare for families earning up to $69,000 and will make childcare cheaper for households with a combined income of $174,000 or less.

HEADLINE: Catalano set for Nine's regional newspapers
TEXT:
Antony Catalano is set to ink one of the biggest deals of his career as he emerged as the clear front-runner to buy Nine's extensive suite of regional newspapers.

As Street Talk first reported last night, it's believed Mr Catalano, who is backed by Thorney Assest Management billionaire Alex Waislitz, could sign a deal to buy the division as early as today. In 2011, Mr Catalano sold half of his stake in real estate classified business Domain to Fairfax Media for $35 million. He left his role as Domain chief executive in early 2018 and later tried to scuttle Fairfax's merger with Nine.

Street Talk p15

HEADLINE: Gupta to make 20,000 Aussie electric cars
TEXT:
British billionaire Sanjeev Gupta says the price of electric vehicles will fall steadily like big-screen televisions and solar panels and he's close to finalising plans to become a niche manufacturer in Australia with a likely production run of between 10,000 and 20,000 vehicles.

Mr Gupta, whose GFG Alliance has been working closely with the UK's Gordon Murray Design for the past 18 months on its electric vehicle strategy, says GFG is getting towards the final stages of deciding which of the prototype vehicles it will use to launch into the local marketplace.

Companies p14

HEADLINE: Stan Perron's family has a whole lot more to give
TEXT:
Australia's burgeoning philanthropy industry is about to welcome a new powerhouse into its ranks with the Stan Perron Charitable Trust, run by daughter Elizabeth Perron, set to become one of the country's biggest givers.

Stan Perron, a long-time Rich Lister who continued working almost to the day he died in November aged 96, stipulated in his will that the lion's share of the $200 million-plus in annual profits generated by the Perron Group would flow to the family's foundation.

"I feel privileged to continue his legacy and people have expectations about that legacy continuing as well," Ms Perron told The Australian Financial Review Magazine, in her first media interview. "I think you need to be passionate about it and I've had some really good insight and education into that with Dad."

Stan Perron's fortune was valued at $4 billion in the 2018 Financial Review Rich List. The terms of his will mean that his family will disappear from this year's Rich List. Instead their foundation is expected to rocket up the ranks of the Financial Review Philanthropy 50 list, which tracks the donations by the country's largest foundations and private givers.

Perron Group managing director Ross Robertson said up to 50 per cent of annual profits - or about $100 million a year based on recent financial performance - would eventually flow to the foundation, but this will be a steady build over time based on Mr Perron's wishes to make sure the money finds a good projects. He said over time as the foundation scales up it would probably sit within the top ranks of the Philanthropy 50 list, which has been led by the Paul Ramsay Foundation, the Ian Potter Foundation and Andrew Forrest's Minderoo Foundation. The Perron family's foundation allocated some $12.8 million to causes in 2017-18, putting it at No. 13 on the Philanthropy 50 list.

Ms Perron said not a day went by when she didn't wish her father was still around to offer his advice on the best way forward. They spent the past decade working closely together as he personally assessed and responded to thousands for requests for help from hospitals, medical research centres, child health organisations, families and individuals.

"Over the past 10 years, I have sat with Dad reading and discussing the letters of request and listening to presentations from individuals and groups seeking support," Ms Perron said. "It has been a special time to spend with my Dad. I have learned, on the job, the business of the foundation and in particular the causes that mattered most to him."

Knowing there would be so much more money flowing to the foundation and many more people to help after his passing, Mr Perron also left a roadmap for his daughter to follow.

"As a result the foundation, won't be making any radical changes. I want to honour my father's legacy and his commitment to WA and in particular to children," she said.

"However, we don't have any set targets or prescribed formulas. My intention would be to remain open and flexible to new projects and applications whilst respecting my father's wishes and guidelines."

In addition to her big job as chair of the foundation, Ms Perron has been a director of the Perron Group since 1996 and is just back from her first trip to Japan in her new role as chair of Toyota WA. The Perron Group derives its profits from substantial interests in retail and commercial property, exclusive rights to Toyota vehicle and parts distribution in Western Australia, unlisted airports, Rio Tinto iron ore royalties, residential land development, managed equites and unlisted infrastructure funds.

The 52-year-old mother of two young adult daughters is also managing to do something her father warned she wouldn't have time for - volunteering as a Lifeline crisis supporter.

The volunteer work sees Ms Perron answering Lifeline calls for four hours every week in what she described as another way to help and connect with people rather than financially giving.

The Financial Review Philanthropy 50, in association with JBWere, will be published inside The Australian Financial Review Magazine, on www.afr.com and inside the Financial Review on May 3.

My intention would be to remain open and flexible to new projects.Elizabeth Perron

HEADLINE: Feisty debate sets election race alight
TEXT:
Bill Shorten has acknowledged some voters will be unhappy with Labor's tax agenda but said "there was a mood for change in Australia" and closing "tax loopholes" was essential to guarantee equality and essential services.

Scott Morrison warned the economy faced uncertain times ahead as he urged voters to take into account the past 5½ years of jobs growth and that the budget was on track to return to surplus under the Coalition.

In their first head-to-head debate of the election campaign last night, the two leaders, in a robust but civil debate, both guaranteed the days of dumping leaders were over and whoever won on May 18 would be prime minister for the next three years.

"I lead a united and stable team and we've been working on the policies to ensure Australia's future is a fantastic one," Mr Shorten said.

Mr Morrison said both parties had changed their rules to prevent further coups. "They can't happen again and they shouldn't happen again."

"The prime minister they elect will be the prime minister who will serve over the next three years."

The debate, held in front of a live audience of 48 undecided voters in Perth, featured significant discussion over climate change, with the Prime Minister demanding Mr Shorten detail the economic cost of his more ambitious plan.

The Labor leader said it was not possible "to give one number" but "you do have to spend money" to combat the problem.

"We're going to take on the government's scare campaigns because if we don't, we are selling out the future," he said. "If we don't take real action on climate change, it will be a disaster for our economy."

Labor, which has a 45 per cent emissions reduction target on 2005 levels by 2030, has promised an economy-wide approach to climate change. It includes a baseline and credit scheme for the nation's 250 heaviest emitters, measures to encourage the uptake of electric vehicles, land-clearing restrictions and a household battery subsidy scheme for the energy sector.

The Coalition, which has a 26 to 28 per cent target, will spend $2 billion over 10 years paying polluters to reduce emissions.

Mr Morrison said Labor's emission reduction policies and high tax agenda would harm the economy and wages growth.

He argued the best way to fund essential services and improve people's lives was by ensuring strong economic growth. "Our plan is to keep that going because we are facing stiff headwinds into the future for our economy," he said.

Mr Shorten said his plans to increase taxes and end tax concessions were vital to fund better health and education systems, help lift wages and ensure a fairer society.

"We can afford to pay for these because we've made the hard decisions going forward," he said.

"None of this can happen if we keep the same government in power."

He acknowledged the unpopularity of some of Labor's proposals, which include ending cash refunds for excess franking credits and curbing negative gearing, capital gains tax deductions and the use of trusts.

"We acknowledge that some people won't be happy but what we want to do is to stop providing tax loopholes to the top end of town and those who are already very well off, and instead we prioritise childcare costs, the pensions, hospitals and schools," he said.

He and Mr Morrison clashed over franking credits. Mr Morrison said Mr Shorten was not telling the truth when he said pensioners and part-pensioners were not affected. The exemption for pensioners and part-pensioners only applies to a cut-off in March last year.

Mr Shorten said the cash payments were unsustainable.

"This nation can't keep giving money in the form of a tax cheque to people who didn't pay tax," he said.

Mr Morrison spruiked his credentials as the immigration minister who stopped the boats. Mr Shorten said Labor too, wouldn't weaken border security. Mr Morrison dismissed this, saying Labor would abolish temporary protection visas, which it last did in August 2008. "That's when the boats started to come," he said.

They clashed over preference deals with Mr Shorten saying Mr Morrison had made the Coalition beholden to Clive Palmer and Pauline Hanson, while Mr Morrison said Labor would be in cahoots with the Greens and their agenda which includes death taxes.

The debate was held in Perth where Labor is hoping to take four seats from the Coalition - Stirling, Swan, Hasluck and Pearce, the latter of which is held by Attorney-General Christian Porter.

The men squared off on the back of the latest Newspoll, which showed Labor leading by just 51 per cent to 49 per cent on a two-party preferred basis. The two parties have not been this close since just before Malcolm Turnbull was deposed in August last year.

While Mr Shorten fared well in the debate, there was more uncertainty from the Labor leader earlier yesterday when he would not rule out subsidising other low-paid, female dominated sectors by saying childcare workers would be "first".

"Wages are stagnating, that's a fact. This government has broken records no government wants to break in terms of wages. That's a problem," he said.

"We have picked childcare workers to go first. I think this is a strategically important industry."

Mr Shorten said taxpayer-funded wage subsidies would not be economy-wide but nor did he say they would be confined only to childcare. "No, I don't see this as economy-wide, this approach at all," he said. "I do accept in certain sectors of the economy we have a wages problem. Don't we?"

Mr Morrison blasted the wage subsidy policy, which will culminate in an $11,300 annual wage rise after eight years, costing $537 million over four years and $9.9 billion over 10 years.

"What about construction workers that are being paid the same, men and women? What about people in the retail industry? What about people who are hairdressers? Is he going to subsidise their wages too?' he said.

"Is this how Bill Shorten is going to run the economy? Is he going to set everybody's wages and if he doesn't like what they are getting paid, is he going to tax people more to send the money to them?"

HEADLINE: GetSwift's boardroom implosion
TEXT:
It is possible the founders of software logistics company GetSwift, Bane Hunter and Joel Macdonald, are smarter than their track record with a public company has shown them to be.

Just because their actions landed the company with multiple shareholder class actions, civil penalty proceedings against them by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and the destruction of Australian institutional investor confidence in the company does not mean Hunter and Macdonald are ignorant and reckless executives.

Nor does the implosion in the boardroom of GetSwift last week, which saw the chairman and two other independent non-executive directors depart without warning, signal that Hunter and Macdonald have no time for traditional forms of corporate governance.

The company told the ASX it wants to appoint two new non-executive directors "with significant experience generating revenues and scaling commercial operations for growth".

This looked distinctly like a slap in the face for the three directors who left on Friday - chairman Michael Fricklas, Belinda Gibson and David Ryan. Fricklas said the three left because they have "different views as to the manner in which the company engages with its board".

This is code for saying there was a boardroom fight and the majority of independent directors lost.

Nevertheless, it's possible to read into the company's statement about the importance of revenue and commercial imperatives of a recognition by Hunter and Macdonald that their approach up to this point has not been fit for purpose.

The scorecard of their commercial success is contained in two years of quarterly reports, and it's not pretty. The company's progress towards profitability has been at a snail's pace. Receipts from customers in the December quarter of last year, at $170,000, were about the same as the receipts from customers in the September quarter of 2017.

Since then the costs of running the business have soared from $574,000 to $5.8 million. The company's cash burn is rising sharply, mostly because of the legal costs involved in fighting the shareholder class actions and the ASIC civil penalty cases.

The receipts from customers more than doubled in the March quarter compared to previously thanks to the acquisition of two companies in the United States - delivery management platform Delivery BIZ Pro and the acquisition of popular workforce scheduling provider, Scheduling+ for $6.6 million.

It is dangerous sticking your neck out with compliments for Hunter and Macdonald given their track record, but it would seem they have done well with these transactions.

Assuming the additional revenue secured in the March quarter of about $250,000 came from the two new acquisitions, it would seem GetSwift paid about six times annual revenue. GetSwift trades on about 20 times revenue from customers.

At this stage readers might ask why Chanticleer is bothering about GetSwift, a company worth $40 million in a listed technology sector comprising 200 companies worth $90 billion.

Why spend any time at all on a stock with rapidly diminishing interest from institutional investors and retail shareholders who have been repeatedly burnt by negative announcements out of left field.

GetSwift is actually a perfect case study for the times. It provides useful insights into a number of important issues, including corporate governance of volatile tech stocks, class action response strategies for directors, and the consequences of ASIC's litigate first approach.

On the question of corporate governance, it is not known what really happened inside the GetSwift boardroom. But it is certain the directors, reflecting the views of shareholders, were out of step with Hunter and Macdonald.

Several institutional shareholders have told Chanticleer they want the company to settle the class actions and move on. They want to stop the cash bleeding out to lawyers and instead get Hunter and Macdonald to focus on the business.

Hunter and Macdonald live and work in New York so they may not realise the damage done to their institutional shareholder base from past actions. Institutional shareholders have been voting with their feet by selling the stock.

IFM Investors and Fidelity were both substantial shareholders in the company but they have cut their holdings. Regal Funds Management remains a substantial shareholder.

The company has two strong supporters in the US - Clutterbuck Capital Management LLC and the founder of KPT Capital LLC. They issued a statement in early April saying they were highly supportive.

They said it was essential Hunter and Macdonald remained "at the helm for many reasons, including their strong customer relationships, deep industry expertise, and the ability to attract and retain key talent".

But the two shareholders said their faith in the company's governance was founded on having Fricklas as chairman.

Class actions have become part of corporate life in Australia largely because ASIC decided to outsource the enforcement of corporate disclosure obligations to litigation funders. No class action case in Australia has gone to trial. All have been settled.

This points to the GetSwift class action being settled at some stage. Why not settle it as soon as possible instead of burning cash?

ASIC's decision to launch civil proceedings against GetSwift and Hunter and Macdonald in February was unusual. ASIC alleges the company misled the market when it failed to notify the ASX of material information in relation to its client agreements.

ASIC contends that Hunter and Macdonald were either involved in the failure of GetSwift to meet its obligations and failed to discharge their duties to GetSwift with the requisite degree of care and diligence that a reasonable person in their respective positions would exercise.

The ASIC case will go to trial in June 2020. In other words, it will be 2½ years since the alleged breaches of the disclosure laws occurred.

As ASIC seeks to establish its reputation as a tough enforcer of the law under commissioner Daniel Crennan, it won't be able to get quick results. It will have to rely on legal action announcements to show it is effective rather than actual convictions.

GetSwift is burning through its cash as it spends more on lawyers and ramps up its hiring of software engineers and spends more on research and development. It has enough cash to last about 16 months based on its latest cash-burn rates. That won't leave much in the till for shareholders if the class action proceeds and the defendants lose.

TONY BOYD

HEADLINE: Lendlease looks higher for Docklands tower
TEXT:
Development and construction player Lendlease has upscaled its plan for a $1 billion commercial tower in Melbourne's Docklands, taking heart from the city's tight office market to increase the building by five levels.

The property giant had already won state government approval for what will be the commercial centrepiece of the $2.5 billion Melbourne Quarter precinct on the edge of Docklands, overlooking the old CBD grid.

But in an unusual move, Lendlease has gone back to the drawing board, bringing in architectural firm Woods Bagot to redesign the tower, taking it from 137 metres to more than 165 metres high.

The revised plan for Melbourne Quarter Tower has already won endorsement from Town Hall and Lendlease will now seek approval for the changes from the state government.

"We continue to see strong demand for high-quality office space in the market and are confident that Melbourne Quarter Tower - located directly opposite Southern Cross Station and completing Melbourne Quarter's Collins Street precinct - will lease strongly," a Lendlease spokeswoman said.

The construction value of the tower is estimated at $380 million. Fully developed and tenanted the tower could be worth about $1 billion.

At 31 storeys, the tower would comprise 65,000 square metres of net leasing area.

Lendlease's decision to go higher reflects the listed player's view of the future of supply of office space and demand for it in the central city.

Melbourne's CBD is now the tightest office market in the country after vacancy slipped further from 3.6 per cent to 3.2 per cent in February.

In a separate super-development next door, property magnate Lang Walker this month signed the final tenant for his Collins Square project, making the $2.5 billion multi-tower project fully leased.

Stretching from Flinders Street to Collins Street, Lendlease's Melbourne Quarter precinct has three office buildings along with apartment towers.

The first tower, One Melbourne Quarter, is now fully leased with tenants including Arup, AMP and Lendlease itself. Co-working hub operator Spaces has also signed up.

More than half of the 50,000sq m Two Melbourne Quarter, now under construction, has been committed to tenants including EnergyAustralia.

Under the new Woods Bagot design, the floor plate of the third and largest office building, Melbourne Quarter Tower, has been modified from a regular rectangle. The revised plan includes convex curves on two facades.

HEADLINE: Mother drives from Port to live near son in Bendigo
TEXT:
We speak to the team behind the most intriguing recent property sale.

The property: A four-bedroom house at 19 Orlando Street, Eaglehawk [Bendigo], Vic. Sold by private treaty for $410,000.

Who was the agent/agency? Brent Mason, Ray White Bendigo.

How long was this on the market? [Brent] It wasn't. It never got to the market. It was meant to go live that night online. But because they offered what I thought was a good price and the vendor was pretty happy with, we didn't hit the net.

Why did this one sell? The purchaser has an emotional connection to the street. It wouldn't have mattered if it was Number #19 or Number #1 as long as it was close to her son in the street and she could live close to her son.

Was it overpriced? No. We appraised it at between $400,000 to $420,000. Feedback from the vendor was that he would have kept it if anyone offered below $400,000 and kept it as a rental.

What did you think it would go for? Me personally? Probably $400,000.

What was surprising about it?

It's not every day that the next-door neighbour's mother, who doesn't even live in town - that's just baffling - rings off a signboard, having driven all those kilometres for two days, inspects a property, pretty much signs a contract on the spot and buys in an unconditional form.

The signboard went up on a Friday. I get a call from an old lady moving from Port Macquarie who mentioned her son lives in the area. She said her son was driving past the property and noticed the signboard.

She was wondering if she could inspect the property after getting to Bendigo on the Monday after her long drive in the camper trailer.

She and her husband rocked up. When she was in the inspection I asked her "What are your thoughts?"

She said "Tell Dan I will put the money in his account tomorrow."

I'd never even mentioned the vendor's name.

She said "We were talking to his mum across the road. I was letting them know I will buy the property today. We'll settle ASAP." She said they'd pay $400,000 and I said "That's not going to cut it". Then she said maximum price she would pay was $410,000.

Later that night, I rang the vendor and said: "We need to catch up." He said: "It's funny you called. That group you showed through are my next-door neighbour's parents".

They'd already gone back to the property before I had contacted the seller. The buyers had knocked on the door to discuss the price for the fridge and table and chairs.

She was so grey about it. She said: "My son has driven past this property and noticed the signboard". She never once said: "My son lives next door and has seen the sign board go up."

This family now owns three properties in a row. The son also owns the property on the corner of Orlando and Burnside. They own pretty much half the street.

Do you reckon we'll see another result like this: a) next week b) next year c) next cycle d) never?

d) I don't think I'll ever see another sale like this ever again in my real estate career. I hope I do, but don't think I will.
